blocks.heading: What providers assess
blocks.text: A finance provider examines the proposal from its own risk and return perspective. Banks and other lenders assess ability to repay principal and interest, using expected cash flows, trading history, existing debt, management and any security offered. Security may reduce loss if repayment fails but does not prove the business can make instalments. Shareholders consider potential dividends and growth in the value of their investment, risks, management quality and the rights or influence offered. Institutional lenders or development bodies can also apply mandate and eligibility conditions, such as the project purpose, beneficiaries or environmental requirements stated in a programme. A borrower’s wish for low interest does not explain why a provider would accept the risk. Distinguish the requested amount from evidence that it is sustainable. Strong evidence can improve the likelihood of funding, but the final decision also depends on the provider’s criteria and available funds.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Eha Panels asks a bank for a machine loan. Its customer orders look promising, but existing repayments already absorb much of its cash. The bank should examine the timing and reliability of receipts against both existing and proposed commitments. Promising sales alone may not leave enough cash for the new instalments. Eha’s desire for a low rate is a borrower preference, not evidence of repayment capacity.

blocks.heading: Banks as providers
blocks.text: Banks supplying loans examine repayment capacity, expected cash flows, existing debt, the purpose and term of the loan, management reliability and security where relevant. Interest compensates the bank for supplying funds and bearing risk, but a higher offered rate does not automatically make a weak borrower acceptable. Collateral is a possible fallback if the borrower defaults, not a substitute for reliable operating cash. The borrowing enterprise’s limited liability normally limits owners’ exposure, which can leave the lender exposed rather than protect it. Assess the enterprise and any expressly agreed additional security.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Mavo Joinery has assets available as security but forecasts a cash shortage during the proposed repayment months. The security could reduce loss in default, yet the forecast raises doubt about on-time repayment. The bank may require a revised schedule, more evidence or decline the proposal; possessing an asset alone does not establish approval.

blocks.heading: Shareholders as providers
blocks.text: Shareholders supply equity in exchange for an ownership interest. They assess potential dividends, longer-term growth in value, the chance of losing their investment, management quality and the voting or other rights offered. Equity does not promise the scheduled interest and capital repayments of a loan. Expected profit may support future dividends, but dividends depend on available resources and decisions, not a guaranteed fixed payment. An investor may reject an attractive sales story if costs, risk or ownership terms are unclear.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ota Foods offers an investor a minority share interest to fund equipment. Sales are forecast to rise, but proposed distributions and voting rights have not been explained. The investor needs expected profit and risk information as well as clear ownership rights. Increased revenue does not establish the dividend return, because costs and retention decisions intervene.

blocks.heading: Institutions as providers
blocks.text: Institutions providing finance assess whether a proposal fits the type of funding and their stated mandate. A development institution may examine eligibility, project viability, likely benefits and the applicant’s contribution; an institutional lender also examines repayment and risk. Grants can require spending on a specified activity and evidence of compliance. Conditions differ, so use the programme facts provided instead of assuming every institution supplies free or interest-free funds. A socially useful proposal can still be ineligible or financially unviable.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Assume a fictional enterprise-support institution offers equipment funding to eligible new manufacturers, with a required applicant contribution. A retailer applies without that contribution. The retailer’s application does not fit the stated activity and contribution conditions. Its need for equipment is not enough to establish eligibility. The institution must assess its own rules as well as the applicant’s enthusiasm.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Finance needs, sources and provider criteria
blocks.text:
Fictional Nali Milling needs N$120,000 for equipment lasting several years and N$15,000 for materials before customers pay. It has N$20,000 genuinely spare retained cash after protecting its operating reserve. A bank is considering a term loan for equipment and a supplier may allow short credit for materials. Repayment capacity and agreed terms must still be assessed.

a(i) State two needs for finance shown for Nali. [2]
a(ii) State two factors a lender considers before supplying funds. [2]
b State two other circumstances that can create a business need for finance. [2]
c Explain why a term loan may suit Nali’s equipment while supplier credit may suit its materials. [6]
d Evaluate whether a bank should rely on the forecast rise in sales alone to approve Nali’s loan. [8]

a(i) Purchasing the equipment and paying for materials before receipts arrive. a(ii) Repayment cash flows and existing borrowing commitments. b Starting operations and replacing a failed essential asset. c Equipment gives benefits over several years, so a suitable term loan can spread repayment across the period in which it helps generate cash. Supplier credit delays material payment during the shorter customer-payment gap, if its due date fits receipts. Long-lived equipment should not depend on a short credit deadline the business cannot meet. d Higher forecast sales may support repayment if they convert into sufficient cash, but sales could be uncertain, delayed or accompanied by higher costs. The bank should assess cash timing, existing debt, management and security where relevant. Do not approve on sales alone; decide after a credible repayment assessment. The borrower’s need for equipment does not itself show the lender that the loan is safe.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Finance needs, sources and provider criteria
blocks.text:
Fictional Nali Milling needs N$120,000 for equipment lasting several years and N$15,000 for materials before customers pay. It has N$20,000 genuinely spare retained cash after protecting its operating reserve. A bank is considering a term loan for equipment and a supplier may allow short credit for materials. Repayment capacity and agreed terms must still be assessed.

a Explain why Nali has two different finance needs and how the bank and supplier would assess them. [8]
b Evaluate using retained cash alone compared with a combination of internal and external finance. [12]

a The equipment is a long-term investment need and the materials are a short operating-cash need before customers pay. A bank offering a term loan needs evidence that instalments and interest fit the cash flows, including existing commitments. The supplier needs confidence that payment will arrive on its credit deadline; customer receipts delayed beyond that date would create risk. The owner’s desire for a cheap source is different from either provider’s assessment. Terms should match timing and amount rather than merely the word finance. b Nali has N$20,000 spare against N$135,000 of stated needs, so retained cash alone cannot meet them. Internal funds avoid new loan interest and preserve ownership, but draining its essential reserve would create operating risk. A combination can use some spare funds and match a suitable equipment loan and supplier credit to their distinct durations. It adds repayment obligations and depends on agreement and cash affordability. Choose the combination if the bank and supplier terms fit credible receipts and the operating reserve remains protected. If finance is not affordable, postpone or reduce the investment rather than treating borrowing as guaranteed.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Finance needs, sources and provider criteria
blocks.text:
Fictional Tawa Repairs needs N$60,000 for a machine. It has N$65,000 retained cash after its essential operating reserve and forecasts stable receipts. It compares using that spare cash with a bank loan carrying interest. No alternative use is identified for these spare funds. For part (b) only, most retained cash has now been committed to an essential roof repair, leaving N$10,000 spare after the operating reserve. The N$60,000 machine need and expected receipts are unchanged.

a Evaluate internal retained cash against a bank loan under Tawa’s original facts. Include the finance need and provider perspective. [12]
b Evaluate the same choice after the essential roof commitment changes the spare cash available. Explain whether the judgement changes. [12]

a Tawa needs long-term equipment finance, not a loan for its own sake. Genuinely spare retained cash of N$65,000 can cover the N$60,000 price while the essential reserve stays protected. It avoids interest and preserves control, though it reduces funds available for unexpected events. A loan could preserve spare liquidity but adds commitments; the bank would assess expected cash, existing debts and risk. Prefer internal cash given stable receipts and no stated competing use, while reviewing the forecast before spending. b N$10,000 spare cannot fund a N$60,000 machine. The change removes the sufficiency condition behind the original recommendation. A suitable term loan or mixed funding becomes more relevant if machine benefits support repayment and the bank accepts the evidence. Avoid using cash needed for the essential roof or operating reserve. Change towards external or mixed finance subject to affordable terms; if those terms are unavailable, postpone the machine. Need alone does not establish repayment capacity.
